script.opening: "I came about my headaches really, but… there’s something else. My parents are taking me abroad in the summer holidays. They say it’s just to see family, but I overheard them, and I think they’re planning for me to marry a man over there. I don’t want to. I’m really scared. Please don’t tell them I told you."

facts.text: On the video call from a small private room at school during lunch; the school nurse helped her book it and set it up. Nobody else is in the room. Her parents don’t know about the appointment.

"I heard them talking about a wedding over there, and it was about me." Two weeks ago her mother was on the phone to an aunt about "the arrangements" and a man’s name she didn’t know. Her older cousin was married abroad at 17 "and never came back to school". Nobody has asked Sana what she wants.

"When school finishes for the summer" — in about 5 weeks. They haven’t said how long. Her father keeps the family passports; "I don’t know where it is." She has a photo of her passport on her phone (only if asked).
"Nobody’s hurt me. I just can’t talk to them about it." Not locked in; phone is checked sometimes. Feels OK to go home tonight. No self-harm, no suicidal thoughts: "I just want it to stop."
Evening headaches for a month, "when I’m worrying". No morning headaches, no vomiting, no vision problems, no weakness. Takes paracetamol sometimes.
"No one. You’re the first person." Trusts her form tutor and the school nurse. Has a best friend, Amira, but hasn’t told her.
Year 11, doing well, wants to do A levels and become a pharmacist. Lives with parents, two younger brothers and her grandmother. English is spoken at home and she speaks it fluently.

Quiet, frightened, keeps glancing at the door. Repeatedly ask that your parents not be told. If the doctor suggests talking to your parents or "family mediation", panic and say you have to go. If the doctor is calm, believes you and explains that they will help without telling your parents, agree to a referral and to being contacted through school. Ask: "Will they go to my house?"

ice.ideas: "They’re going to make me marry someone over there."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "If anyone finds out I told, they’ll take me sooner. Or I’ll just never come back." She is terrified of losing school and her future.
ice.expectations: "I don’t know. Help me without them knowing."

cues: "Please don’t tell them I told you" — never involve the family; explain confidentiality and its limits honestly.
"When school finishes for the summer" — imminent travel; act now (one chance).
"I came about my headaches really" — the presenting complaint was a way in.

checkpoints.text: Recognises FORCED MARRIAGE as ABUSE and a SAFEGUARDING/child-protection issue (and a criminal offence — 2014 Act; and under the 2022 Act, in force 27 February 2023, any marriage of a child under 18 is an offence, no coercion needed, including non-legal ceremonies), distinct from an arranged marriage between consenting adults, and takes the disclosure seriously
Applies the ONE-CHANCE RULE — acting sensitively but DECISIVELY at this consultation (she may not present again) — and sees her ALONE

Does NOT contact/involve the FAMILY, NOT use family/community members as interpreters, and does NOT attempt MEDIATION/family counselling or send letters/calls to the family home (which endanger her; The Right to Choose 2023)
Assesses RISK and safety (imminent travel/timing, passport, threats/coercion, prior siblings, restriction of freedom, safety tonight, self-harm) and reassures her she did the right thing

Follows local SAFEGUARDING procedures URGENTLY (safeguarding lead, children’s social care, police if imminent), involves the FORCED MARRIAGE UNIT/specialist support (knowing an FMPO can prevent removal), documents, and gives practical safety advice with a safe contact route and code word
Responds with sensitivity and belief, maintains appropriate confidentiality while acting on the safeguarding duty, and supports a frightened young person
Lets her tell her story at her own pace and believes her, and explains clearly what will happen next and why the family cannot be involved, so she feels safe and in control of the process
Reaches a safe plan: urgent safeguarding referral, FMU involvement, no family contact/mediation, risk assessment, documentation and support — the one-chance rule applied, not deferred or mediated

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me — that took real courage, and I’m really glad you did. You’ve done absolutely the right thing. You’re safe here, and we’re seeing you on your own. Let’s work out how to help you."

"What you’re describing — being made to marry against your will — is called forced marriage. It’s not the same as an arranged marriage you agree to; it’s a form of abuse and against the law — and since 2023 it’s a crime for anyone to arrange for someone under 18 to be married, here or abroad, even in a religious ceremony — and protecting you is my priority."

"I want to reassure you: I will NOT contact your parents or talk to your family about this, and I won’t try to mediate — that could put you in danger. I do need to be honest that, because you’re 16 and at risk of serious harm, I have to share this with children’s social care, and I’ll tell you exactly what I share. This stays handled carefully and safely."

"Can you tell me when the trip is planned, and whether anyone’s threatened you or watches where you go? Who has your passport? Has this happened to a sister or cousin? Do you feel safe going home tonight, and have you ever thought about hurting yourself because of this? That helps me judge how urgent this is."

"I’m going to get specialist help involved straight away — our safeguarding team and the people who protect young people, and a national service called the Forced Marriage Unit. They’re experts at keeping you safe, including if travel is imminent — there’s a court order called a Forced Marriage Protection Order that can stop anyone taking you abroad."

"Let’s agree a safe way for us to contact you — school might be safer than your phone — and a code word. Take a photo of your passport and keep it with someone you trust, and I’ll give you who to contact in an emergency — if you’re ever taken to an airport against your will, you can tell border staff. We’ll make a plan together and I’ll document this carefully, in your own words. I’d also like to hear briefly about the headaches. You are not alone in this."

f.learning: FORCED MARRIAGE (a marriage entered into without one or both parties’ free and full CONSENT, involving coercion) is a form of ABUSE, a SAFEGUARDING/child-protection issue, and a criminal offence (s121 Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014; and since 27 February 2023, under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022, causing a child under 18 to marry is an offence in England and Wales without any need for coercion, including non-legal ceremonies) — distinct from an ARRANGED marriage between consenting adults — and a disclosure (often made indirectly under another pretext) must be taken extremely seriously. The critical principle is the "ONE-CHANCE RULE": the young person may have only one opportunity to disclose and seek help and may not present again (they could be taken abroad), so act sensitively but DECISIVELY at this consultation, seeing them ALONE. Essential safeguards: do NOT contact or involve the FAMILY, do NOT use family or community members as interpreters (use a professional interpreter), and do NOT attempt MEDIATION, family counselling or "talking to the parents", or send letters or make calls to the family home — these can place the person at serious risk (The Right to Choose, statutory guidance 2023) (escalation, being taken abroad sooner, harm). Assess risk and safety (imminent travel plans and timing, passport, threats/coercion, prior siblings forced, restriction of freedom, self-harm), reassure them they have done the right thing, and follow local SAFEGUARDING procedures urgently — involving the safeguarding lead and a same-day children’s social care referral (and police if imminent risk; Working Together 2023) — and seek advice from the FORCED MARRIAGE UNIT and specialist support (a Forced Marriage Protection Order under the Family Law Act 1996 can prevent removal), maintaining confidentiality appropriately while acting on the safeguarding duty, documenting carefully, and giving practical safety advice (a safe contact route and code word, a copy of the passport kept safe, emergency contacts, what to do if taken to an airport) and briefly assessing the headaches. The skill is recognising forced marriage, the one-chance rule, NOT involving family/mediation, and urgent safeguarding/FMU referral.

knowledge.guideline: [1] Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, s121 (forced marriage offence) · [2] Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022 (in force 27 February 2023) · [3] Family Law Act 1996 Part 4A: Forced Marriage Protection Orders · [4] HM Government, The Right to Choose: multi-agency statutory guidance for dealing with forced marriage and multi-agency practice guidelines (Forced Marriage Unit, 2023) · [5] GMC Protecting children and young people (2012) and GMC Confidentiality (2017) · [6] Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023)
knowledge.summary: A 16-year-old who fears being taken abroad to be married is a child at risk of significant harm. In England and Wales, since 27 February 2023, it is a crime to do anything intended to cause a child under 18 to marry, whether or not coercion is used, and this includes non-legally-binding religious or cultural ceremonies [1, 2]. The GP must see her alone, believe her, apply the ‘one chance’ principle, never involve or alert the family, and refer to children’s social care the same day (police on 999 if travel or harm is imminent), with advice from the Forced Marriage Unit [4]. A Forced Marriage Protection Order can prevent her removal from the UK [3].

points.t: Using violence, threats or any other coercion to cause someone to marry, or deceiving someone into going abroad for that purpose, is an offence under s121 of the 2014 Act [1], maximum 7 years. The 2022 Act [2] raised the minimum age of marriage and civil partnership to 18 in England and Wales and made it an offence to cause a child to marry, with no need to prove coercion and including ceremonies not recognised in law. An arranged marriage between consenting adults is lawful; at 16 there is no lawful marriage to arrange.

Under Part 4A of the Family Law Act 1996 [3], the family court can make an FMPO to protect a person at risk, for example by ordering surrender of passports or forbidding travel. The person, a local authority or others with the court’s permission can apply; orders can be made urgently and without notice to the family. Breaching an FMPO is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).

The statutory guidance [4] warns that professionals may have only one chance to speak to a potential victim. Act at this consultation: see her alone, in a safe place, take a full account, and do not send her home to ‘think about it’ without a safety plan and referral.

The guidance [4] lists actions that can put a victim at greater risk: involving the family, community or religious leaders; family counselling, mediation, arbitration or reconciliation; using relatives, friends or community members as interpreters; and sharing information with anyone without careful consideration. Use a professional interpreter and do not send letters or make calls to the family home.

Refer to children’s social care the same day under local procedures and Working Together [6]; call 999 if she is in immediate danger or travel is imminent. Seek advice from the Forced Marriage Unit (FCDO and Home Office), which supports professionals and victims [4]. GMC guidance [5]: share information to protect a child at risk of significant harm, telling her what you will share and why unless that would increase the risk. Record her words verbatim and store the record securely.

Agree a safe way and time to contact her, and a code word. Advise her to keep a copy of her passport and key documents somewhere safe, and emergency numbers memorised. If she is taken to an airport against her will she can tell airport security or police. British nationals abroad can contact the nearest British embassy or high commission; the FMU can assist overseas [4].

model.text: Hello Sana, I’m Dr Hughes. Before we start — are you somewhere private where nobody can overhear? … Good. What would you like to talk about today?

I came about my headaches really, but… there’s something else. My parents are taking me abroad in the summer holidays. They say it’s just to see family, but I overheard them, and I think they’re planning for me to marry a man over there. I don’t want to. I’m really scared. Please don’t tell them I told you.

Thank you for telling me. That took real courage, and I’m glad you did. This call is private, and it’s just you and me. I won’t be speaking to your parents about this. Can you tell me more about what you heard?
model.why: Believes her; confirms she is alone; immediate reassurance about the family

model.text: I heard them talking about a wedding over there, and it was about me. Nobody has asked me.
When is the trip, and do you know which country and for how long?
model.why: Timing of travel: the key to urgency

model.text: When school finishes for the summer. They haven’t said how long.
Who has your passport at the moment?
I don’t know where it is.
Has anyone threatened you, hurt you, or stopped you going out, using your phone or seeing friends?
Nobody’s hurt me. I just can’t talk to them about it.
Has anything like this happened to a sister, cousin or anyone else in the family?
model.why: Prior family history of forced marriage

model.text: Not that I know of.
Do you feel safe going home tonight? And have you ever thought about hurting yourself because of this?
I think it’s OK tonight. I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want it to stop.
Is there anyone you trust, at school or anywhere else, who knows about this?
No one. You’re the first person.
What are you most frightened of right now?
That if anyone finds out I told, they’ll take me sooner. Or I’ll just never come back.
And what were you hoping I might do?
I don’t know. Help me without them knowing.

What you’re describing is called forced marriage. It’s against the law in this country, and since 2023 it’s a crime for anyone to arrange for someone under 18 to be married, here or abroad, even in a religious ceremony. None of this is your fault.
model.why: Names it; explains the 2022 Act for under-18s

model.text: Even if it’s not official?

Yes, even then. My job is to keep you safe, and I need to be honest with you about how. Because you’re 16 and at risk of serious harm, I have to share this with the people whose job is to protect young people: children’s social care. I’ll tell you exactly what I share. I will not contact your parents, and they will not be told by me that you came here.
model.why: Explains the duty to share honestly, with limits

model.text: Will they go to my house?

They are trained in exactly this situation and know not to put you at risk by going to your family without a plan. They can involve the police, and there is a court order called a Forced Marriage Protection Order which can stop anyone taking you abroad, for example by holding passports. There’s also a government team called the Forced Marriage Unit that advises us and you.
model.why: Explains FMPO and FMU in plain words

model.text: Here’s what I’d like to do. While you’re here, I’ll ring our safeguarding lead and children’s social care. Is it all right for you to wait with me while I do that?
model.why: Acts in this consultation: the one chance principle

model.text: OK. As long as my parents don’t find out.
What’s a safe way for someone to contact you? Is your phone private, or would school be safer? We can also agree a code word, so if you ever call and say it, we know you need help.
model.why: Safe contact method and code word

model.text: School, I suppose. That would be safer than home.

If you can, take a photo of your passport and keep it with a trusted person. If you’re ever taken to an airport and don’t want to go, tell airport security or police. If you’re abroad, the British embassy can help. And if you’re in danger at any time, call 999.

About the headaches: I’d like to hear about them briefly, and get your blood pressure and eyes checked — the practice nurse and an optician can do that without anyone needing to know why. Stress like this can cause headaches, but I don’t want to ignore them.
They’re just in the evenings, when I’m worrying.
I’ll write down only what you’ve told me, in your own words, in a secure part of your record. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
You’re calling social care now, they’ll contact me through school, not my parents, I keep a copy of my passport, and I call 999 if it’s urgent.
Exactly. You’ve done the right thing, Sana. You’re not on your own with this.

social.t: Forced marriage often sits within honour-based abuse. Victims fear rejection by family and community as much as the marriage, which shapes what support feels possible.
School is often the safest route of contact and a source of trusted adults; children’s social care can coordinate with the designated safeguarding lead.

legal.t: Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 s121: forced marriage offence, including deception to take someone abroad (maximum 7 years). Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022: minimum age 18 in England and Wales; causing a child to marry is an offence without proof of coercion.
Family Law Act 1996 Part 4A: civil orders, available urgently and without notice, e.g. passport surrender or travel bans. Breach is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).
Children Act 1989 and Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023): refer a child at risk of significant harm to children’s social care.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017) and Protecting children and young people: disclose to protect a child from serious harm; tell her what will be shared unless that increases risk; share the minimum necessary with the right agencies.
Use a professional interpreter, never family or community members. Record her words verbatim; protect the record from access by relatives, including online record access.

community.t: Forced Marriage Unit (FCDO and Home Office) for professionals and victims; specialist honour-based abuse charities; Childline; the British embassy or high commission if abroad.

pitfalls.intro: The clinical content is small; the station is about decisive safeguarding in a single chance. Marks are lost for anything that alerts the family, for false promises, and for sending her away without a plan.

items.fail: Suggesting a conversation with her parents, a family meeting or mediation.
items.why: The statutory guidance identifies family involvement and mediation as increasing risk.
items.fix: No family contact of any kind; refer to children’s social care.

items.fail: Deferring action to a later appointment.
items.why: The one chance principle: she may be taken abroad before she returns.
items.fix: Make the referral while she is with you.

items.fail: Not asking about travel dates, passport and threats.
items.why: These decide how urgent the response must be and whether police or an FMPO are needed.

items.fail: Treating it as lawful because she is 16 or because it may be ‘only religious’.
items.why: Since February 2023 causing a child to marry is an offence in England and Wales, including non-legal ceremonies.
A referral will follow; a broken promise destroys trust.
items.fix: Explain honestly what you will share, with whom, and why.

items.fail: No safe contact plan, or ignoring the headaches.
items.why: Letters or calls home can expose her; the presenting complaint still needs attention.
items.fix: Agree contact via school and a code word; briefly assess the headaches.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as a family disagreement, suggests talking to her parents or mediation, promises total secrecy, or sends her away to ‘think about it’.
wordPics.pass: Sees her alone, believes her, assesses travel risk, explains the need to share, refers to children’s social care and mentions the FMU, and gives safety advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: acts within the consultation (one chance), explains the 2022 Act and FMPOs, agrees a safe contact route and code word, avoids any family contact including letters or calls home, addresses the headaches, and documents verbatim and securely.

avoid.dont: “Would it help if I had a word with your mum and dad?”
avoid.instead: “I won’t contact your parents. The people who help with this know how to keep you safe.”
avoid.why: Involving the family or mediation can escalate the risk; the statutory guidance advises against it.

avoid.dont: “Everything you tell me is completely confidential.”
avoid.instead: “Most of what we talk about stays private, but when a young person is at risk of serious harm I have to share it to protect you. I’ll tell you what I share.”
avoid.why: False promises destroy trust when a referral follows; GMC guidance supports sharing to protect a child.

avoid.dont: “Have a think and come back next week.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s make the calls now, while you’re here.”
avoid.why: She may not get another chance to disclose.

SCA_MODELS.text: School, I suppose. That would be safer than home.

If you can, take a photo of your passport and keep it with a trusted person. If you’re ever taken to an airport and don’t want to go, tell airport security or police. If you’re abroad, the British embassy can help. And if you’re in danger at any time, call 999.

About the headaches: I’d like to hear about them briefly, and get your blood pressure and eyes checked — the practice nurse and an optician can do that without anyone needing to know why. Stress like this can cause headaches, but I don’t want to ignore them.
They’re just in the evenings, when I’m worrying.
I’ll write down only what you’ve told me, in your own words, in a secure part of your record. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
You’re calling social care now, they’ll contact me through school, not my parents, I keep a copy of my passport, and I call 999 if it’s urgent.
Exactly. You’ve done the right thing, Sana. You’re not on your own with this.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, s121 (forced marriage offence) · [2] Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022 (in force 27 February 2023) · [3] Family Law Act 1996 Part 4A: Forced Marriage Protection Orders · [4] HM Government, The Right to Choose: multi-agency statutory guidance for dealing with forced marriage and multi-agency practice guidelines (Forced Marriage Unit, 2023) · [5] GMC Protecting children and young people (2012) and GMC Confidentiality (2017) · [6] Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 16-year-old who fears being taken abroad to be married is a child at risk of significant harm. In England and Wales, since 27 February 2023, it is a crime to do anything intended to cause a child under 18 to marry, whether or not coercion is used, and this includes non-legally-binding religious or cultural ceremonies [1, 2]. The GP must see her alone, believe her, apply the ‘one chance’ principle, never involve or alert the family, and refer to children’s social care the same day (police on 999 if travel or harm is imminent), with advice from the Forced Marriage Unit [4]. A Forced Marriage Protection Order can prevent her removal from the UK [3].

points.t: Using violence, threats or any other coercion to cause someone to marry, or deceiving someone into going abroad for that purpose, is an offence under s121 of the 2014 Act [1], maximum 7 years. The 2022 Act [2] raised the minimum age of marriage and civil partnership to 18 in England and Wales and made it an offence to cause a child to marry, with no need to prove coercion and including ceremonies not recognised in law. An arranged marriage between consenting adults is lawful; at 16 there is no lawful marriage to arrange.

Under Part 4A of the Family Law Act 1996 [3], the family court can make an FMPO to protect a person at risk, for example by ordering surrender of passports or forbidding travel. The person, a local authority or others with the court’s permission can apply; orders can be made urgently and without notice to the family. Breaching an FMPO is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).

The statutory guidance [4] warns that professionals may have only one chance to speak to a potential victim. Act at this consultation: see her alone, in a safe place, take a full account, and do not send her home to ‘think about it’ without a safety plan and referral.

The guidance [4] lists actions that can put a victim at greater risk: involving the family, community or religious leaders; family counselling, mediation, arbitration or reconciliation; using relatives, friends or community members as interpreters; and sharing information with anyone without careful consideration. Use a professional interpreter and do not send letters or make calls to the family home.

Refer to children’s social care the same day under local procedures and Working Together [6]; call 999 if she is in immediate danger or travel is imminent. Seek advice from the Forced Marriage Unit (FCDO and Home Office), which supports professionals and victims [4]. GMC guidance [5]: share information to protect a child at risk of significant harm, telling her what you will share and why unless that would increase the risk. Record her words verbatim and store the record securely.

Agree a safe way and time to contact her, and a code word. Advise her to keep a copy of her passport and key documents somewhere safe, and emergency numbers memorised. If she is taken to an airport against her will she can tell airport security or police. British nationals abroad can contact the nearest British embassy or high commission; the FMU can assist overseas [4].

social.t: Forced marriage often sits within honour-based abuse. Victims fear rejection by family and community as much as the marriage, which shapes what support feels possible.
School is often the safest route of contact and a source of trusted adults; children’s social care can coordinate with the designated safeguarding lead.

legal.t: Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 s121: forced marriage offence, including deception to take someone abroad (maximum 7 years). Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022: minimum age 18 in England and Wales; causing a child to marry is an offence without proof of coercion.
Family Law Act 1996 Part 4A: civil orders, available urgently and without notice, e.g. passport surrender or travel bans. Breach is a criminal offence (maximum 5 years).
Children Act 1989 and Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023): refer a child at risk of significant harm to children’s social care.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017) and Protecting children and young people: disclose to protect a child from serious harm; tell her what will be shared unless that increases risk; share the minimum necessary with the right agencies.
Use a professional interpreter, never family or community members. Record her words verbatim; protect the record from access by relatives, including online record access.

community.t: Forced Marriage Unit (FCDO and Home Office) for professionals and victims; specialist honour-based abuse charities; Childline; the British embassy or high commission if abroad.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical content is small; the station is about decisive safeguarding in a single chance. Marks are lost for anything that alerts the family, for false promises, and for sending her away without a plan.

items.fail: Suggesting a conversation with her parents, a family meeting or mediation.
items.why: The statutory guidance identifies family involvement and mediation as increasing risk.
items.fix: No family contact of any kind; refer to children’s social care.

items.fail: Deferring action to a later appointment.
items.why: The one chance principle: she may be taken abroad before she returns.
items.fix: Make the referral while she is with you.

items.fail: Not asking about travel dates, passport and threats.
items.why: These decide how urgent the response must be and whether police or an FMPO are needed.

items.fail: Treating it as lawful because she is 16 or because it may be ‘only religious’.
items.why: Since February 2023 causing a child to marry is an offence in England and Wales, including non-legal ceremonies.
A referral will follow; a broken promise destroys trust.
items.fix: Explain honestly what you will share, with whom, and why.

items.fail: No safe contact plan, or ignoring the headaches.
items.why: Letters or calls home can expose her; the presenting complaint still needs attention.
